items.stem: A generated Python script uses a bare 'except: pass' around a data-loading step. Why is this a problem?

options.text: It hides errors so a failed load can silently produce wrong results
options.rationale: Correct: swallowing exceptions masks failures and corrupts downstream results.

options.text: Bare except runs faster than specific handling
options.rationale: Performance is not the issue; silent failure is.
except is valid Python; the problem is swallowing the error.
It does the opposite: it suppresses the crash and hides the fault.

items.explanation: Correct: swallowing exceptions masks failures and corrupts downstream results.

items.stem: Which TWO checks validate a CSV join transformation? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Compare row counts before and after against expectations
options.rationale: Correct: unexpected row counts reveal dropped or duplicated rows.

options.text: Reconcile a key total against the source export
options.rationale: Correct: totals confirm the transformation preserved the data.

options.text: Confirm the script printed the word 'done'
options.rationale: A success message is not evidence the data is correct.

options.text: Check that the output file name is shorter
options.rationale: File name length is irrelevant to correctness.

items.explanation: Correct: unexpected row counts reveal dropped or duplicated rows.

items.stem: An automation script overwrites production data and could be run twice by mistake. The safest design is to:

options.text: Make it idempotent and add a dry-run before destructive operations
options.rationale: Correct: idempotency and dry-run protect against accidental re-runs.

options.text: Run it faster so the window for mistakes is smaller
options.rationale: Speed does not prevent a destructive double-run.

options.text: Remove all logging to reduce clutter
options.rationale: Less logging makes failures harder to detect, not safer.

options.text: Trust the operator never to re-run it
options.rationale: Relying on perfect operators is not a safety design.

items.explanation: Correct: idempotency and dry-run protect against accidental re-runs.
